title: Control Plane: operator scenarios and routing decisions
content:
Purpose and scope

Quick / messy operator-focused notes to capture ownership edges between API gateway, orchestrator, and runtime adapters when we need to make fast routing decisions across regions and capacity tiers. This is a working doc (notes, scenarios, operator actions, and TODOs) — intended for platform on-call and platform-ownership syncs.

Audience
- Platform engineers (on-call)
- SREs who escalate to platform
- Product/platform PMs who make rollout decisions

High-level problem statement
We expose a unified Redwood API surface but traffic may traverse multiple control-plane components: ingress/API gateway -> orchestration service (route decision + rollout rules) -> runtime adapters (model routing, quantization variant selection, regional endpoints). During partial failures, capacity constraints, or multi-region cutovers we must coordinate fast decisions with clear ownership. Operational ambiguity causes: 1) conflicting fallbacks, 2) double-counted quotas, 3) silent latency regressions. This doc enumerates operator scenarios and recommends clear actions and owners.

Service responsibilities (short operator cheat-sheet)
- API Gateway (team: eng-gateway):
  - Accepts/validates client requests, enforces auth/quotas at the route level, applies global rate-limits.
  - Fast-fail for malformed or obviously rate-limited requests.
  - Emits ingress-level latency metrics and request traces.
  - Owner for TLS, ingress scaling, WAF rules.

- Orchestrator (team: eng-orchestration):
  - Decision point: given request metadata, selects target model variant, region, and adapter pool.
  - Responsible for rollout policies (canary %, A/B), fallback policy table (region fallback, model-family fallback).
  - Enforces routing constraints (tier-based routing, geo restrictions).
  - Owner for policy config, rollout state, and feature flags.

- Runtime Adapters (team: eng-serving-runtime):
  - Translate orchestration decisions into adapter-specific invocation (batching, quantized binary selection), maintain health status for adapter pools.
  - Implement per-pool throttles and backpressure signals to orchestrator.
  - Owner for adapter health, kernel/quantization compatibility, and pool capacity reports.

- Cache Service (team: eng-storage-cache):
  - Prefix/KV caching for repeated prompts. Acts as optional short-circuit for low-latency responses.
  - Owner for cache eviction policies and metrics.

- Quota & Billing (team: eng-platform-ops):
  - Enforces tenant quotas after gateway acceptance, reconciles usage with billing, emits billing metrics.

Common ambiguity zones (where operators need clear guidance)
1) Fallback ownership: if orchestrator routes to fallback region because adapter pool signals degraded, who marks the request for billing in the fallback region? Answer: Quota & Billing uses the final invoke record produced by runtime adapters. Gateway still records ingress counters.
2) Double-fallback: gateway-level DNS failover + orchestrator fallback becomes a double-hop. Operator action: disable gateway DNS failover if orchestrator-managed cross-region fallback is enabled for the route.
3) Cache vs Adapter consistency: stale cache hits may serve older model outputs (version mismatch). Owner: cache service must validate model-version header with orchestrator during cache set; runtime adapters must insert model-version header on successful execution.

Operator scenarios and playbook (step-by-step)
Scenario A: Single-region adapter pool overload (high latency, 503s)\- Detection: adapter pool health shows increased tail latency and 5xx; orchestrator marks pool degraded, orchestrator metrics show increased queue depth. Alert: ORCH-HighLatency-Pool.\- Immediate operator actions:\ 1) Confirm degradation in runtime-adapter dashboard (owner: eng-serving-runtime).\ 2) Orchestrator should automatically reroute to secondary variant or region per policy (if enabled). If automatic reroute did not happen, operator triggers manual policy flip in orchestrator (owner: eng-orchestration).\ 3) If reroute elevated latency for some tenants, gate via rollout % (orchestrator).\ 4) Notify gateway team if ingress rate needs to be temporarily rate-limited or traffic shaped (owner: eng-gateway).\- Post-incident follow-up:\ 1) Root cause (resource exhaustion, bad kernel, network blips).\ 2) Add a protective rollout rule: auto-throttle when queue depth > X.

Scenario B: Regional cloud outage (us-east-1) with live Dedicated customers pinned to region\- Detection: broad service degradation, region metrics down, health probes failing.\- Immediate operator actions:\ 1) Assess customer pinning/constraints via orchestrator UI (owner: eng-orchestration + customer success).\ 2) If customer is pinned and cannot be moved, escalate to sales/CS and SREs for mitigation; raise incident call.\ 3) For unpinned traffic: orchestrator should reroute to next-best region per cost/latency tradeoff. If orchestrator policy disallows cross-region fallback for specific workloads (compliance), mark those requests as impacted and route to degraded response path.\ 4) Gateway DNS failover must be checked: if DNS cutover already in place, coordinate rollback with gateway owners to avoid routing loops.\- Post-incident:\ 1) Review pinned-customer policy and disaster-playbook for pinned capacity (customer-failover contracts).

Scenario C: Orchestrator policy bug causes routing loops (orchestrator->adapter->orchestrator retry)\- Detection: amplified traffic spikes, repeated traces showing same request id hitting orchestrator multiple times. Alert: ORCH-Routing-Loop.\- Immediate operator actions:\ 1) Quarantine the offending policy in orchestrator (owner: eng-orchestration).\ 2) Pause retries at gateway-level if possible (owner: eng-gateway).\ 3) Scale down orchestrator evaluation workers if loops cause control-plane CPU exhaustion.\ 4) Check runtime adapters for idempotency and request dedupe.\- Post-incident: add automatic loop detection (trace cycles > 2) and circuit-breaker in orchestrator.

Decision matrix: who does what in 90s, 10min, 60min windows\- 90s:\  - API Gateway: emit ingress metrics, fast-fail traffic waves, apply emergency rate-limits.\  - Runtime Adapters: update health flags to orchestrator.\  - Orchestrator: evaluate automatic fallback and execute if policy exists.\- 10min:\  - Platform on-call (primary): decide manual reroutes and brief stakeholders.\  - Gateway: temporarily reduce global rate for noisy tenants.\  - Serving runtime: triage kernel/adapter failures and consider draining pool.\- 60min:\  - Cross-team incident call, customer notifications, escalate to product & sales for pinned customers.\  - Config changes (rollout policy adjustments) applied with small percentages first.

Routing policy examples (pseudocode)
- Geo-first failover policy:\  if region.available and latency < 200ms then route(region) else route(nearest_region_with_capacity)
- Cost-aware fallback:\  prefer cheaper variant if latency delta < 50ms and predicted token cost reduces by >10%
- Compliance-lock:\  if tenant.requires_data_residency then restrict(route) to tenant.region_pools

Operational invariants (must hold)
1) Orchestrator is the single source-of-truth for routing decisions. If gateway has a conflicting routing behavior it must be explicitly labeled and justified.
2) Runtime adapters must always report final invoke metadata (region, adapter-id, model-version, tokens) for billing reconciliation.
3) No silent double-billing: billing uses adapter final records, but gateway counters are used for rate-limits only.

Observability checklist for on-call\- Dashboards: ingress-qps, ingress-5xx, orchestrator-decision-latency, adapter-pool-tail-latency, adapter-5xx-rate, cache-hit-rate.\- Traces: end-to-end trace correlated by request id; ensure orchestrator decision span is present and annotated with policy id.\- Alerts: ORCH-Decision-Latency, ADAPTER-Pool-Health, GATEWAY-Rate-Limit-Surge, CACHE-Thundering-Herd.

Runbook excerpts (fast commands)\- Force a policy rollback in orchestrator (console link): ORCH console -> policies -> rollback to previous stable -> apply with 5% ramp. (owner: eng-orchestration)\- Remove gateway DNS failover: gateway console -> route -> toggle DNS-failover=false -> confirm with prod-dns. (owner: eng-gateway)\- Quarantine adapter pool: runtime console -> pool -> mark unhealthy -> drain -> notify. (owner: eng-serving-runtime)

Open questions / TODOs\- TODO: Add policy schema v2 to make fallbacks declarative and composable (work item: JIRA-PLAT-1501).\- Question: Should orchestrator own tenant-level sticky-routing (session affinity) or should that live at the gateway? Proposal: orchestrator owns affinity for model-version stickiness; gateway can implement short-lived sticky sessions for connection-affinity.\- TODO: Add a canonical field in trace that indicates final billing region (to remove ambiguity).\- TODO: Write e2e chaos test that simulates adapter pool flapping + orchestrator rollback and validate no customer traffic is double-counted.

Post-incident action items (owners)
- Add auto-circuit-breaker for routing loops (owner: Priya / eng-orchestration) – due 2025-02-15\- Add model-version header enforcement for cache entries (owner: Marco / eng-storage-cache) – due 2025-02-28\- Policy schema draft v2 (owner: Aaron / eng-platform) – due 2025-03-10

Notes and references
- Keep this doc intentionally practical — aim to capture the immediate operational decisions rather than architecture-only diagrams.
- For the canonical architecture and past ownership maps, see Confluence: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/PLAT/Control+Plane+Topology\- Related PRs: https://github.com/redwood-inference/control-plane/pull/789

Changelog\- 2025-01-10: created (initial scenarios and actions)\- 2025-02-02: added decision matrix, runbook commands, and open TODOs

End of doc
